2026-09-08.title: Your Computer Is Basically a Very Fast Idiot
2026-09-08.subtitle: It renders movies, runs games, and holds video calls — by doing one mind-numbingly simple thing a few billion times a second.

tg_quiz.q: What's the CPU's one job?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — one dumb loop, billions of times a second.
tg_quiz.wrong: Nope — it just loops: fetch, decode, execute.
tg_quiz.explain: Everything 'smart' is that tiny loop stacked into a tower.

2026-09-08.title: Money Is a Story We All Agree to Believe
2026-09-08.subtitle: The cash in your pocket is worthless paper. The number in your bank isn't even paper. So why does the whole world chase it?

tg_quiz.q: What actually backs a modern banknote?
options: Shared trust that others will accept it
tg_quiz.correct: Exactly — money is a story we all agree to believe.
tg_quiz.wrong: Not gold — it's collective trust, backed by law.
tg_quiz.explain: Value lives in the network of people who accept it, not the paper.

2026-09-08.title: Stop Thinking in Yes/No. Start Thinking in Odds.
2026-09-08.subtitle: Almost nothing is certain, yet your brain demands a yes or a no. Learning to answer in numbers is the single biggest upgrade to how you think.

tg_quiz.q: Flip a fair coin twice — chance of heads both times?
tg_quiz.correct: Nice — AND means multiply: ½ × ½ = ¼.
tg_quiz.wrong: Close — for 'both', multiply: ½ × ½ = ¼.
tg_quiz.explain: Independent events combine by multiplying.

2026-09-09.title: The Worst Good Idea in Human History
2026-09-09.subtitle: Planting seeds made us sicker, shorter, and more overworked than our ancestors. It also built literally everything. Both things are true.

tg_quiz.q: Farming's real superpower was…
tg_quiz.correct: Yes — surplus is what built civilization.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's surplus — the leftover food that freed people to specialize.
tg_quiz.explain: No surplus, no specialists, no cities.

2026-09-09.title: Your Blazing-Fast Computer Spends Most of Its Life Waiting
2026-09-09.subtitle: Yesterday we met the CPU that does billions of things a second. So why is software ever slow? Because the data is stuck in traffic.

tg_quiz.q: RAM vs L1 cache — roughly how much slower?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — about 100× slower. Location is everything.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's ~100× slower — seconds vs minutes in human time.
tg_quiz.explain: Which is why caches keep hot data close to the CPU.

2026-09-09.title: The Most Important Curve in Finance (It Prints Money While You Sleep)
2026-09-09.subtitle: Would you take $100 now or $100 next year? Pin down *why* you said 'now' and you've unlocked how to value almost anything.

tg_quiz.q: $100 at 10%, compounded — after 2 years?
tg_quiz.correct: Nice — $121. That extra $1 is interest on interest.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's $121 — you earn 10% on $110, not just the original $100.
tg_quiz.explain: Compounding: interest earns interest.

2026-09-10.title: Bayes' Theorem: How to Change Your Mind Without Losing It
2026-09-10.subtitle: New evidence lands. How much should it move you? There's an exact answer — and it's the most useful formula you'll ever internalize.

tg_quiz.q: Rare disease (1/1000), 99%-accurate test, you test positive. Chance you're actually sick?
tg_quiz.correct: Exactly — ~9%. False positives swamp the rare true case.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's ~9% — the disease is so rare that most positives are false alarms.
tg_quiz.explain: Always weigh evidence against the base rate. That's Bayes.

2026-09-10.title: Humanity's First Killer App Was a Spreadsheet
2026-09-10.subtitle: The earliest writing isn't poetry or scripture. It's receipts — lists of grain and sheep. And that boring origin explains everything.

tg_quiz.q: The world's oldest writing was mostly…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — receipts and tallies. History's first spreadsheet.
tg_quiz.wrong: It was accounting — grain, sheep, and taxes, not poetry.
tg_quiz.explain: Writing was invented to track surplus, not to tell stories.

2026-09-10.title: The Choice That Makes Code 1,000× Faster (or Slower)
2026-09-10.subtitle: Same computer, same data, same task — but pick the wrong way to store your stuff and it grinds to a halt. Meet Big-O.

tg_quiz.q: 10× the data into an O(n²) algorithm ≈ how much slower?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — 100×. Quadratic bites hard at scale.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's 100× — (10)². That's why O(n²) is a trap.
tg_quiz.explain: Big-O is about how cost grows, not the raw clock.

2026-09-11.title: How to Put a Price on the Future
2026-09-11.subtitle: A company is worth the cash it'll throw off for years. A bond is a stream of future payments. So how do you price a river of money that hasn't arrived yet?

tg_quiz.q: Rates jump. The present value of far-future cash…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — a higher discount rate shrinks future money.
tg_quiz.wrong: It falls — bigger r means future cash is worth less today.
tg_quiz.explain: Why rate hikes hit long-duration assets (like tech stocks) hardest.

2026-09-11.title: Expected Value: The Math Behind Every Good Decision
2026-09-11.subtitle: Should you take the bet, buy the insurance, launch the product? One little calculation cuts through the fog — and pros run it constantly.

tg_quiz.q: 10% chance to win $50. Expected value of the prize?
tg_quiz.wrong: It's $5 — probability × payoff = 0.10 × $50.
tg_quiz.explain: If it costs more than $5 to play, it's a losing bet on average.

2026-09-11.title: The Bronze Age Internet
2026-09-11.subtitle: 4,000 years ago, tin from Afghanistan met copper from Cyprus to make bronze — via a trade web so tangled its collapse ended an age.

tg_quiz.q: Why did bronze force long-distance trade?
options: Tin & copper are rarely in the same place
It was too heavy to keep
tg_quiz.correct: Right — you had to connect distant mines to make it.
tg_quiz.wrong: Because tin and copper rarely occur together — trade connected the mines.
tg_quiz.explain: Bronze literally required a trade network to exist.

2026-09-12.title: Why Doing Two Things at Once Breaks Everything
2026-09-12.subtitle: Run two bits of code at the same time and they can trip over each other in ways that vanish the moment you look. Welcome to concurrency.

tg_quiz.q: Two $100 withdrawals hit a $100 balance at once, both read before either writes. Result?
tg_quiz.correct: Exactly — that's a race condition (lost update).
tg_quiz.wrong: Both read $100 first, so both approve — $200 out. That's a race condition.
tg_quiz.explain: A lock makes the read-decide-write atomic so this can't happen.

2026-09-12.title: There's No Free Lunch: Risk and Return
2026-09-12.subtitle: Anyone promising high returns with no risk is lying or confused. Understand the trade-off and you'll never fall for it.

tg_quiz.q: "Guaranteed 15% a year, zero risk" — what is it?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — risk-free excess return doesn't last. Classic scam signal.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's a red flag — real returns come with real risk.
tg_quiz.explain: No free lunch: reward requires risk.

2026-09-12.title: How We Accidentally Invented Government
2026-09-12.subtitle: Nobody sat down and designed the state. It grew out of grain, walls, and the need to manage more people than anyone could know.

tg_quiz.q: The state essentially arose to…
options: Let strangers cooperate at scale (defense, disputes, infrastructure)
tg_quiz.correct: Right — impersonal machinery for people who can't all know each other.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's about scaling cooperation among strangers — law, taxes, bureaucracy.
tg_quiz.explain: Personal trust doesn't scale to a city; institutions do.

2026-09-13.title: Your Brain Runs on Shortcuts (And They Betray You)
2026-09-13.subtitle: Evolution built you a fast, lazy autopilot that's brilliant most of the time and predictably, hilariously wrong the rest.

tg_quiz.q: Bat + ball = $1.10; bat is $1 more than the ball. The ball costs…
tg_quiz.correct: Nice — you engaged System 2. It's 5 cents.
tg_quiz.wrong: System 1 says 10¢, but it's 5¢ (ball 5¢ + bat $1.05 = $1.10).
tg_quiz.explain: The gut answer feels right and is wrong — that's the whole lesson.

2026-09-13.title: What Actually Happens When You Open a Link
2026-09-13.subtitle: You tap a link and a page appears. In between, your request crosses the planet and back through a dozen machines — in under a second.

tg_quiz.q: What's DNS?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — it turns names into the numbers routers use.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the phone book: it maps a name to an IP address.
tg_quiz.explain: Names for humans, numbers for routing.

2026-09-13.title: The Only Free Lunch in Investing
2026-09-13.subtitle: Yesterday: no reward without risk. Today: the one trick that lets you cut risk without cutting expected return. Economists literally call it the only free lunch.

tg_quiz.q: Which is genuinely diversified?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — diversification needs things that don't move together.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the mixed one — 10 tech stocks all crash together.
tg_quiz.explain: Low correlation is what makes the noise cancel.

2026-09-14.title: Why Some Nations Are Rich and Others Aren't
2026-09-14.subtitle: Same geography, same resources, wildly different fortunes. The best answer isn't culture or climate — it's the rules of the game.

tg_quiz.q: Two towns, same desert & ancestry, one much richer. Biggest reason?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — the rules of the game, not the resources.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's institutions — the rules people live under, not geography.
tg_quiz.explain: Inclusive rules invite investment; extractive ones smother it.

2026-09-14.title: How to Spot a Bad Argument in Two Seconds
2026-09-14.subtitle: Most persuasion that fools us isn't lying about facts — it's cheating on logic. Learn the common cheats and you can't be conned the same way twice.

tg_quiz.q: 'Either we ban this completely or society collapses.' Which fallacy?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — false dilemma: pretending only two options exist.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's a false dilemma — it fakes an either/or when more options exist.
tg_quiz.explain: Real choices rarely come in just two flavors.

2026-09-14.title: "There Are Only Two Hard Problems in Computer Science"
2026-09-14.subtitle: …cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors. The joke is famous because caching really is that treacherous — and that essential.

tg_quiz.q: The famously 'hard' part of caching is…
options: Invalidation (knowing when the copy is stale)
tg_quiz.correct: Right — cache invalidation, the classic hard problem.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's invalidation — deciding when the cached copy has gone stale.
tg_quiz.explain: Too eager loses speed; too lazy serves wrong data.

2026-09-15.title: Nobody Sets the Price. Everybody Does.
2026-09-15.subtitle: No committee decides what a coffee, a stock, or a house is worth. A price is a signal that emerges from millions of buyers and sellers haggling at once.

tg_quiz.q: Who sets the 'right' price of a coffee?
options: No one — it emerges from supply & demand
tg_quiz.correct: Right — it emerges where supply meets demand.
tg_quiz.wrong: No single person — it emerges from buyers and sellers together.
tg_quiz.explain: A price is a signal, not a decree.

2026-09-15.title: The Printing Press: History's First Viral Moment
2026-09-15.subtitle: One machine dropped the cost of copying an idea by orders of magnitude — and toppled churches, sparked science, and remade Europe.

tg_quiz.q: The printing press's core effect was to collapse the cost of…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — cheap copies let ideas escape the elite.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the cost of copying ideas — that's what changed everything.
tg_quiz.explain: Cheap distribution → Reformation, science, mass literacy.

2026-09-15.title: Why Your Brain Can't Feel Exponential Growth
2026-09-15.subtitle: Fold a paper 42 times and it reaches the Moon. Your gut says 'a few inches.' That gap explains pandemics, compound interest, and viral everything.

tg_quiz.q: Fold 0.1mm paper 42 times — roughly how far?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — to the Moon. Exponentials break intuition.
tg_quiz.wrong: To the Moon! Doubling 42 times explodes far beyond gut feeling.
tg_quiz.explain: Linear brain, exponential world.

2026-09-16.title: How Databases Find a Needle in a Billion-Row Haystack
2026-09-16.subtitle: A database can find one record among a billion in milliseconds. The secret is the same idea behind a book's index — and a clever tree.

tg_quiz.q: A DB finds 1 row among a billion fast because of…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — an index turns O(n) into ~O(log n).
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the index — a B-tree gets there in ~30 steps, not a billion.
tg_quiz.explain: Like a book's index: look up, jump straight there.

2026-09-16.title: The Recession Alarm Hidden in the Bond Market
2026-09-16.subtitle: Bonds are just loans you can trade. Line up their interest rates and you get a curve that has predicted almost every US recession for 50 years.

tg_quiz.q: An 'inverted' yield curve means…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — short above long, the classic alarm.
tg_quiz.wrong: Inversion = short-term yields ABOVE long-term. A recession signal.
tg_quiz.explain: It's flagged almost every US recession since the '60s.

2026-09-16.title: The Scientific Revolution: When We Learned How to Learn
2026-09-16.subtitle: For millennia, 'truth' meant what ancient authorities said. Then a new rule appeared: test it against reality. That rule changed everything.

tg_quiz.q: The Scientific Revolution's big move was…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — reality, not authority, became the referee.
tg_quiz.wrong: It flipped to testing ideas against evidence — the scientific method.
tg_quiz.explain: Repeatable, self-correcting — so knowledge compounds.

2026-09-17.title: Game Theory: When Everyone Acting Smart Makes Everyone Worse Off
2026-09-17.subtitle: Two prisoners, each doing the rational thing, both end up worse than if they'd cooperated. This one puzzle explains arms races, price wars, and climate stalemates.

tg_quiz.q: In the one-shot prisoner's dilemma, the rational outcome is…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — both betray, both worse off. That's the tragedy.
tg_quiz.wrong: Both betray — individually rational, collectively worse. That's the dilemma.
tg_quiz.explain: Repetition + reputation is how real life escapes it.

2026-09-17.title: The CAP Theorem: Pick Two, You Can't Have Three
2026-09-17.subtitle: Spread data across many machines and physics forces a brutal choice: when the network splits, do you stay consistent or stay available? You can't do both.

tg_quiz.q: When a distributed system's network splits, CAP forces a choice between…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — C vs A. You can't keep both during a partition.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's Consistency vs Availability — partitions force the pick.
tg_quiz.explain: Banks pick C; social feeds pick A.

2026-09-17.title: What Is a Company Actually Worth?
2026-09-17.subtitle: A stock isn't a lottery ticket — it's a sliver of a real business. So its value comes from the cash that business will throw off. Here's how pros pin a number on it.

tg_quiz.q: What most fundamentally determines a company's value?
options: Its future cash flows (discounted to today)
tg_quiz.correct: Right — a business is worth its future cash, brought to today.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the future cash it'll generate, discounted to today.
tg_quiz.explain: Price is what you pay; value is what it's worth.

2026-09-18.title: The Hockey Stick: When Human Life Suddenly Got Better
2026-09-18.subtitle: For thousands of years, almost nothing changed. Then, around 1800, growth went vertical. Understanding that elbow is understanding the modern world.

tg_quiz.q: The Industrial Revolution's core unlock was…
options: Fossil energy (coal + steam) for mechanical work
tg_quiz.correct: Right — energy on demand: one machine, work of hundreds.
tg_quiz.wrong: It was energy — coal + steam turned stored energy into unlimited work.
tg_quiz.explain: Output per person soared past population → the hockey stick.

2026-09-18.title: Feedback Loops: Why Systems Do the Opposite of What You Expect
2026-09-18.subtitle: Push on a complex system and it often pushes back — or spirals out of control. Learn to see the loops and the world stops being baffling.

tg_quiz.q: A thermostat cooling a warming room is which loop?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — balancing: it pushes back toward a target.
tg_quiz.wrong: Balancing — it self-corrects toward a set point (unlike a snowball).
tg_quiz.explain: Reinforcing = amplify; balancing = stabilize.

2026-09-18.title: How a Group of Computers Agrees on Anything
2026-09-18.subtitle: Machines crash, messages get lost, networks split. So how do a dozen servers agree on a single answer — like who owns which seat? Meet consensus.

tg_quiz.q: In Raft, a change is 'committed' once…
options: A majority of machines have stored it
tg_quiz.correct: Right — a majority (quorum) makes it official and crash-tolerant.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's once a majority stores it — that's what tolerates failures safely.
tg_quiz.explain: Overlapping majorities prevent two conflicting leaders.
